profiles.meeting_scenario: At a teaching hospital in Melbourne, the Clinical Skills Unit is reviewing an unexpected pattern from the last two mock accreditation OSCE rounds for internationally trained clinicians: candidates who were coached to 'make the diagnosis explicit to the patient' are giving longer diagnostic statements, using more evidential language, and still missing the keyed diagnosis more often in two high-stakes communication stations. The meeting is a troubleshooting session between the assessment lead and the program's communication analyst to determine whether the problem is caused by station design, coaching language, coding interpretation, or examiner calibration before the next mock exam cycle opens in ten days. The agenda is to compare what each thinks is happening in the recordings, identify the likely root cause of the pattern, and agree on a practical fix for the next round. The expected outcome is a concrete adjustment plan for the mock OSCE process that both believe addresses the problem.

members.name: Dr. Anita Rao
members.expertise: Emergency medicine, OSCE station design, examiner calibration
members.background: An emergency physician who now oversees accreditation practice exams for internationally trained clinicians and is responsible for keeping the mock stations aligned with the formal Australian assessment format.
members.private_state: She wants a fix that can be implemented quickly without reopening the full station bank, and she is especially concerned about anything that could later be interpreted as poor exam design or inconsistent marking.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss 'history-taking time,' they mean the interval from the candidate's first clinical question until the moment the candidate begins summarising or naming the diagnosis.
An 'accurate diagnosis' in this context means the final diagnosis label matches the keyed station answer well enough to earn the diagnostic mark.
References to 'the chest pain station' or 'that respiratory station' point to the current April station version because older pilot variants are no longer decision-relevant in her workflow.
If they agree to 'add a prompt,' it will most naturally mean adjusting examiner guidance or feedback language rather than changing candidate-facing station materials.

members.name: Dr. Lewis Chen
members.expertise: Medical discourse analysis, video-based coding of clinician-patient encounters, communication training
members.background: A linguistically trained health communication researcher embedded in the simulation program who codes OSCE videos and advises on how clinicians phrase explanations, diagnoses, and uncertainty.
members.private_state: He wants the team to avoid simplistic conclusions from the timing data and is quietly trying to preserve a communication-focused interpretation rather than letting the issue be reduced to candidate speed or examiner marking.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss 'history-taking time,' they mean the whole information-gathering phase up to the explicit transition into diagnosis, including recap statements that still function to test or refine the diagnosis.

An 'accurate diagnosis' includes whether the diagnostic statement is warranted, appropriately hedged, and communicatively aligned with the evidence disclosed to the patient, not only whether the keyed label is eventually named.

References to 'the chest pain station' still meaningfully include the March pilot version because the linguistic pattern under discussion originated in those recordings and the station nickname remained unchanged.

If they agree to 'add a prompt,' it will naturally involve candidate-facing wording or standardized-patient cueing, because communication behavior is usually shaped upstream rather than only through examiner notes.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'history-taking time' as if it is a shared timing category from the recordings.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats history-taking time as ending once the candidate starts summarising findings or moves into diagnostic framing, because that is how the exam structure is operationally segmented.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats history-taking time as including recap and confirmatory talk that still functions to gather or test information before the formal naming of a diagnosis.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to timed video review and use the same methodological phrase, so the difference feels like a settled coding convention rather than something needing clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for diagnosis to be accurate
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want to improve 'diagnostic accuracy' or reduce 'diagnostic error.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means increasing the proportion of candidates who state the keyed diagnosis clearly enough to receive the station's diagnostic credit.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means improving whether the diagnosis statement is evidence-based, appropriately calibrated in certainty, and interactionally appropriate for the patient encounter, even if phrased as a likely diagnosis rather than a firm keyed label.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In assessment meetings, 'accuracy' normally sounds objective and shared, and both speakers sincerely believe they are talking about the same clinical outcome rather than different standards for judging it.

misalignment_points.topic: Which station version the problem comes from
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the chest pain station' and 'those recordings' as the source of the troubling pattern.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the current April mock OSCE station version with the revised standardized-patient brief and updated examiner rubric.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking mainly of the March pilot recordings, where the same station nickname was used but the patient cueing and checklist wording were slightly different.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The station keeps the same informal name across versions, and both participants work from memory of recently reviewed videos, so the reference feels obvious and does not trigger version-checking.

misalignment_points.topic: Where the communication prompt will be inserted
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should 'add a prompt' before the next cycle.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means a prompt in examiner calibration notes or post-station feedback so markers reward concise diagnosis delivery consistently.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means a candidate-facing station instruction or standardized-patient cue that shapes how candidates verbally transition into the diagnosis.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In exam operations, 'prompt' is a common shorthand used across checklists, candidate instructions, and SP briefing documents, so agreement on the noun masks disagreement about the implementation channel.

turns.inner_thought: I need a practical explanation that doesn't force us to reopen the station bank ten days out. In the April chest pain station, the pattern looks operationally simple: candidates are moving out of history-taking earlier, then talking too long once they start summarising and naming the diagnosis, and still not landing the keyed diagnosis cleanly enough for credit. If this is framed as examiner inconsistency or a wording issue in coaching, we can fix it quickly. I do not want this to become an argument that the station itself is flawed.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What I'm worried about from the last mock round is the same pattern we flagged in the debrief: candidates seem to be spending less time in history-taking, then much longer in the diagnosis delivery, and we're still not seeing the diagnostic accuracy we'd expect in the chest pain station. Given the next cycle opens in ten days, I'd like us to work out whether that's coming from the coaching language, the way we're reading the recordings, or something in the station process.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want this reduced to 'they're too slow' or 'they just don't know the answer.' In the recordings I'm thinking of, candidates are doing more evidential and interactional work before they commit to a diagnosis statement. To me that's still part of the information-gathering trajectory, not simply a delayed performance problem. The issue may be in how coaching pushes them into a more elaborate diagnostic explanation without helping them manage the transition in talk.
turns.utterance: Yes, and from the recordings, what stood out to me was that the diagnosis section becomes much more evidential. They're verbalising observations, linking pieces together, almost building the case out loud. So I wonder if the pattern is less about knowledge as such and more about how they're transitioning out of history-taking.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—once they start summarising findings, I consider history-taking over, and in April they're getting there too soon. That fits with the coaching message encouraging them to 'make the diagnosis explicit.' They may be stepping into the diagnosis section prematurely, then filling space with explanation and missing the exact label we award. If that's the mechanism, we can tune coaching and marker calibration without touching the station.
turns.utterance: That's how it looks to me as well. In the chest pain station, the history-taking phase feels noticeably shorter before they start summarising and naming the diagnosis, and that does make me wonder whether the coaching is pulling them forward a bit too early.

turns.inner_thought: The chest pain recordings I have in mind are the March pilots, where the candidates often gave very specific observations before committing themselves. That wasn't just overtalk; it reflected uncertainty management with the patient. To me the problem is in the verbalisation of reasoning and how the station ecology elicits that. Anita seems to see the same pattern, so I think we're aligned.
turns.utterance: I agree the chest pain station is the right place to look. In those recordings, candidates often move into quite specific observations before they commit themselves, which makes me think the trouble is in how they're verbalising the diagnostic reasoning rather than simply failing to get there.

turns.inner_thought: For the next round, the target has to be straightforward: improve the proportion who state the keyed diagnosis clearly enough to earn the mark. We do not have time for a broader communication redesign. If they can stop overexplaining once they're in the diagnosis section and land the diagnosis cleanly, the numbers should recover and the station will look stable.
turns.utterance: Right. So for me the immediate goal in the next round is to improve diagnostic accuracy by helping candidates land the diagnosis more cleanly and not overtalk once they're at that point in the encounter.

turns.inner_thought: I'm fine saying 'diagnostic accuracy,' but I mean something slightly richer: the diagnosis statement should be warranted by what has been elicited, calibrated in certainty, and not awkward or abrupt for the patient. If we just compress it into a terse label, we could worsen the communication problem while thinking we've solved it. Still, we can probably shape the statement without arguing over terms today.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely, diagnostic accuracy is the right target. I just think we get there by helping them make a diagnosis statement that's better supported and less interactionally awkward for the patient, especially when their certainty is still emerging.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he agrees on accuracy. The quickest lever is a prompt in examiner calibration notes or feedback language so markers reward a concise, direct diagnosis consistently and faculty stop reinforcing these long diagnostic monologues. I need something we can insert before the next cycle without changing candidate-facing materials or SP scripts.
turns.utterance: Then I think for the next cycle we could add a prompt so candidates stop converting every observation into a long explanation, and so the diagnosis section is marked more consistently.

turns.inner_thought: A prompt is exactly what I was hoping for—something candidate-facing or in the SP cueing that nudges the transition. If we can tell them to state the likely diagnosis in plain language after gathering the key information, that should reduce the evidential sprawl without turning the encounter into a checklist recital. Anita seems on board, which is encouraging.
turns.utterance: I think a prompt would help. Something that nudges them to state the likely diagnosis in plain language after they've gathered the key information from the patient could make that transition less messy.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as we don't touch the station itself. The April revisions already dealt with the noisier cues from earlier drafts, so I can defend leaving the station materials alone. If Lewis is still seeing a communication pattern, then we should be able to solve it through calibration and coaching rather than reopening the April version.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. On the chest pain station specifically, I'm somewhat reassured that the April revisions already removed the noisier cues, so this feels fixable without changing the station itself.

turns.inner_thought: I don't read it as resolved, because in the March chest pain recordings the patient narrative still clearly invited candidates into evidentialised talk before the diagnosis statement. To me that means the cueing problem is still active in the station family, even if Anita thinks the latest version cleaned it up. We may still need upstream wording changes.
turns.utterance: Maybe. The chest pain recordings still make me think the cueing issue is live, because candidates seem to be responding to how the patient narrative invites that evidentialised talk before the diagnosis statement.

turns.inner_thought: I need to lock this down into an operational plan. I'll ask him for a short note on the timing pattern, but in my mind that means the shorter history-taking interval before summarising and diagnosis, and I want the prompt update folded into examiner guidance quickly. If we test that in the next mock and the keyed diagnosis rates improve, we're done.
turns.utterance: All right. Let's keep it tight for this cycle. Can you do a short note on the timing pattern from the recordings, and we'll update the prompt before the next mock run so we can test whether that settles things?

turns.inner_thought: Yes—that gives me room to write up the longer history-taking trajectory as I see it, including how candidates use recap and evidence-linking before diagnosis, and to draft prompt language for the candidate-facing or SP-facing materials. I think we've agreed that the issue is the transition and the diagnosis talk, not merely speed. This seems aligned.
turns.utterance: Yes, I'll draft the note and the prompt language off those recordings and send both through this week. I think we're aligned on what needs adjusting before the next cycle.
